card.band: 4 h. Crowded subject (HTTP/2) and a small case count, so this is likely to be on the easy side: a frontier agent finishes in many trials. The band depends on the fuzzer cases for stream-state and flow-control edge errors. A weaker model fails the HPACK and state-machine buckets.
card.cheat: Using net/http or an h2 crate: the build has no vendored copy and the grader rejects it by import check on the module graph. The hidden fuzzer sequences are not in the image.
card.grading: The verifier runs a built h2spec binary (not in the image) against the server in generic, http2 and hpack groups, plus a generated frame-sequence fuzzer whose expected error codes come from the reference server. Score is the fraction of cases passed over the reference. The agent has a small sample test client.
card.reference: Own reference server written in Go, about 2.5k lines, passing all h2spec cases it should.
card.task: /app ships a TCP-level server skeleton in Go or Rust with no HTTP/2 library. The agent implements framing, HPACK with Huffman and dynamic table, stream state machine, flow control, SETTINGS/GOAWAY/RST_STREAM error handling, CONTINUATION and priority rules, serving fixed responses.
card.title: HTTP/2 server with HPACK passing the h2spec suite

spike_plan.kill_if: Stdlib net/http cannot be blocked without breaking the TCP skeleton, or the stdlib server passes all groups (confirming the cheat and too-easy band).
spike_plan.pass_if: Exact case count is recorded and a net/http-only server passes the bulk of h2spec, which closes the case for the cheat path only if the allowlist can block it; otherwise the task is K11.
steps: In a throwaway Linux container with network, clone summerwind/h2spec at v2.6.0 and build it (smoke build already green, so build is quick).
Run h2spec --dryrun and h2spec --dryrun -S to get the exact case count per group (generic, http2, hpack).
Write a 20-line Go TLS server using only net/http with a fixed 200 handler; run h2spec against it and record per-group pass counts.
Check whether the server passes most cases: if it does, the stdlib path is a working cheat.
Test whether an import allowlist can block net/http and crypto/tls without breaking a raw net.Listen TCP skeleton (go list -deps on a sample main).
Record results and decide whether the task is K11 (cheat unclosable) or K8 (too easy).

v1.summary: The seed is killed as K11 because the Go stdlib HTTP/2 server gives the agent a working path that an import check on the module graph does not block. Even if sealed, the seed's own band note points to K8 (too easy at 4h), and HTTP/2 is on the CROWDED list, so this should not be reworked as-is.
